property_summary: For every call, C.paused() returns the actual stored _paused flag (true when paused, false when not); the mutant inverts this, so for some boolean states the returned value differs.
For any caller, C.paused() returns the actual paused state stored in the contract (i.e., reflects _paused), but the mutant always returns true, so there exist inputs where the returned value differs.

For every address caller, the reference contract's paused() returns the actual stored paused state (false right after initialize when called by any caller), whereas the mutant always returns true — so there exists a caller/address for which paused() differs between reference and mutant.

For every address caller and any prior initialize call status, C.paused() returns the stored _paused boolean (so immediately after initialize it is false and after pause() it is true); the mutant always returns true, so there exist fuzzed inputs (caller and whether pause() was invoked) where paused() differs.

For all callers and any prior sequence of public calls, the reference C.paused() returns the stored _paused flag (so immediately after initialize it is false and after pause() it is true); the mutant always returns true, so there exist fuzzed inputs (choice of whether admin called pause/unpause) where paused() differs.

For every call, paused() must reflect the contract's internal _paused flag (i.e. return true after pause() and false after unpause()); the mutant always returns false, so it will disagree when the contract is paused (paused() should be true but mutant returns false).

For any caller with LRT_MANAGER role, calling pause() sets paused() to true (reference: paused() reflects stored _paused), but the mutant that always returns false will violate this for some fuzzed manager address.

For every address that is granted the manager role and every nonzero lrtConfig address used to initialize C, after calling pause() from that manager the contract's paused() getter must return true (reference) — the mutant that forces paused() to always return false will violate this for some inputs.

After calling pause() (via an account that is allowed to call onlyLRTManager), the reference implementation's paused() must return true for every admissible setup (initialized contract and correct manager role); the mutant that always returns false will violate this for some fuzzed manager / lrtConfig addresses.

After initialize(...) is called with any non-zero lrtConfig address and then pause() is invoked by an account holding the LRT manager role, the reference contract's paused() returns true for every such admissible input; the mutant that makes paused() always return false breaks this property for some inputs.

For any input, the reference contract's paused() returns the actual pause state (false before pause is called) — specifically, immediately after initialization (or without calling pause/unpause) paused() is always false; the mutant returns _isInitializing() instead, which can be true during initialization and thus may return true, violating the rule for some inputs.

For any caller/address, paused() on the correctly implemented contract always equals the stored _paused flag (initially false unless pause/unpause called) — in particular immediately after construction+initialize and without calling pause/unpause it must return false for all inputs; the mutant returns _isInitializing() instead and can return true for some inputs during initialization, violating this rule.

For any address input, calling paused() on the correct contract C always returns false (since we never initialize or pause in the test setup), whereas the mutant may return true for some addresses if it (incorrectly) reads the _initializing flag during construction/initialization; thus paused() must be false for all fuzzed addresses on the reference but can be true on the mutant for some address inputs.

For any address input, calling paused() on the correct contract C (without calling pause/unpause) always returns false; the mutant returns the Initializable _initializing flag instead and can return true for some inputs, so the property is violated for those inputs.

For every address input, calling paused() on a properly deployed and initialized C (initialized via initialize) always returns the stored pause flag value (which remains false if unpaused), whereas the mutant reads _isInitializing() and can return true during initialization — so after proper initialize() completes, paused() must be false for all addresses but the mutant can still return true for some fuzzed addresses/timings.

For any nonzero lrtConfigAddr, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) sets c.lrtConfig() to the provided address; the mutant sets it to address(0) and thus violates this property for some input addresses.

For any nonzero lrtConfigAddr, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) must set c.lrtConfig() to that same address (the reference does; the mutant sets it to address(0) and thus violates this for some inputs).

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) returns (via UpdatedLRTConfig event observable through the public getter lrtConfig()) that c.lrtConfig() equals the provided address; the mutant instead sets lrtConfig to address(0) and so for some non-zero addresses the property breaks.

For any non-zero lrtConfigAddr, calling updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) by an account with the admin role must leave c.lrtConfig() as a non-zero address (the reference stores the provided address; the mutant stores address(0) breaking this), so the property asserts that after updateLRTConfig the stored lrtConfig() != address(0).

For any non-zero address x passed to updateLRTConfig by an admin caller, the contract's lrtConfig() getter returns x (non-zero); the mutant instead sets lrtConfig to address(0) for some inputs, breaking that property.

For any non-zero address input, calling updateLRTConfig(addr) on the correct contract stores lrtConfig to addr (observable via emitting UpdatedLRTConfig and subsequent behavior reading getContract/LRT interactions), whereas the mutant does not update the stored lrtConfig causing the stored lrtConfig getter to remain unchanged after the call for some inputs; the test checks that calling updateLRTConfig actually changes the lrtConfig address when supplied a new non-zero address different from the previous one.

For any non-zero address newConfig different from the current lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(newConfig) on the correct contract stores that address as c.lrtConfig(), but the mutant that omits the assignment leaves c.lrtConfig() unchanged (so there exists inputs where the post-call stored address differs).

For any nonzero newConfig address that is different from the current c.lrtConfig(), calling updateLRTConfig(newConfig) results in c.lrtConfig() equaling newConfig in the reference; the mutant that omits the assignment leaves c.lrtConfig() unchanged for some such inputs, so there exists an input where post-call c.lrtConfig() != newConfig.

For any non-zero newConfig address different from the current lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(newConfig) always updates the stored lrtConfig to that address in the correct contract; the mutant that removes the assignment will fail this rule for some such newConfig values.

For any nonzero address newConfig that is different from the current lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(newConfig) causes the contract's lrtConfig() getter to equal newConfig in the correct contract, whereas the mutant that omits the assignment will leave lrtConfig() unchanged for some such inputs (so there exist inputs where post-call lrtConfig() != newConfig).

For any caller address, calling updateLRTConfig succeeds (does not revert) if and only if the caller has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00) in the referenced lrtConfig; the mutant wrongly requires the MANAGER role so some addresses with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (but not MANAGER) that succeed on the reference will revert on the mutant.

For any caller address that holds DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00) in the configured lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(...) on the reference C always succeeds; the mutant instead requires MANAGER role so some addresses with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE but without MANAGER will be rejected, causing updateLRTConfig to revert.

For any caller address, if the caller has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00) in the configured lrtConfig, updateLRTConfig(...) always succeeds on the correct contract C; the mutant incorrectly checks for MANAGER role instead, so some callers with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE but without MANAGER will be rejected and cause updateLRTConfig to revert.

For any address chosen as the caller and any lrtConfig address, the reference C allows updateLRTConfig(lrtConfigAddr) to succeed exactly when the caller is DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE on the provided lrtConfig; the mutant instead checks MANAGER role causing some inputs (caller holding DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE but not MANAGER) to fail — so the property is that a caller who is DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE can call updateLRTConfig successfully for all inputs in the reference but the mutant rejects at least some such calls.

For any address that has the DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE (0x00) in the configured lrtConfig, calling updateLRTConfig(newAddr) should succeed on the reference contract; the mutant incorrectly checks for MANAGER instead, so some addresses with DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE but without MANAGER will be rejected and cause updateLRTConfig to revert.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the contract's maxNodeDelegatorCount is set to 10 by the reference implementation; the mutant sets it to 0, breaking this invariant for some inputs.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference sets maxNodeDelegatorCount > 0 (specifically 10) while the mutant may set it to 0, so after initialize(address) the getter maxNodeDelegatorCount() must be nonzero — the mutant violates this for some inputs.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize(...), the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (non-zero) after initialization; the mutant sets it to 0 for some inputs, so the invariant 'after initialize, maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 0' holds for the reference for every admissible input but is violated by the mutant for some input.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to a strictly positive value (>0) after initialize completes; the mutant sets it to 0 for some admissible lrtConfig addresses, thereby violating this invariant.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address, after calling initialize(lrtConfigAddr) the reference C leaves maxNodeDelegatorCount equal to 10 (i.e. >= 10), whereas the mutant sets it to 0 for some inputs; the property asserts that after initialize the getter maxNodeDelegatorCount() is >= 10.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize; the mutated contract sets it to 20 for some inputs and thus violates this invariant.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize; the mutant sets it to 20 for some inputs, so the invariant maxNodeDelegatorCount == 10 is violated by the mutant.

For any non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10; the mutant sets it to 20 for some inputs, so the property asserts that after initialize the getter maxNodeDelegatorCount() == 10 (which the buggy version will violate for some fuzzed lrtConfig addresses).

For every non-zero lrtConfig address passed to initialize, the reference C sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to either 10 or a value no less than 10? (We must state a rule the reference always satisfies and the mutant violates) -> General rule: For any non-zero lrtConfig address, after initialize returns successfully the reference contract's maxNodeDelegatorCount is equal to 10; the one-statement mutant that sets it to 20 will violate this for some inputs.

For every non-zero lrtConfig address that allows initialize to return successfully, the reference contract always sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 after initialize; the mutant sets it to 20 for some inputs, so there exists an input where maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 10 causing the property to fail.

After successful initialize(...) by any caller with a non-zero lrtConfigAddr, the reference sets maxNodeDelegatorCount to 10 (non-zero); the mutant omits this assignment leaving it default 0, so there exists an input where c.maxNodeDelegatorCount() != 10 (the fuzzer will find any non-zero address).
